answer.summary: Laura Schaffer recommends iterating and validating ideas quickly with customers, using lightweight tests before investing in full A/B tests. Most hypotheses fail, so early feedback helps teams learn sooner, avoid costly builds, and use failure to guide what to try next.

sections.heading: Iterate and learn early
sections.content: At a high level, Schaffer says it is better to work iteratively than to build something in isolation for months. She says roughly 80% of hypotheses—or, as she also describes it, 80% or more of ideas—are wrong or fail. Getting work in front of customers sooner helps teams catch that earlier; failure can serve as a compass toward a better solution rather than a dead end.

sections.heading: Validate cheaply before A/B testing
sections.content: Because A/B tests can require substantial design, engineering, product or growth work and time to produce results, Schaffer recommends first asking how an idea can be validated quickly. She names painted doors—testing the concept before the experience exists—and design mocks shown to people to see how they engage. Reserve deeper A/B testing for ideas that have been vetted through these earlier methods; this lets teams fail faster and reduces the chance of investing in an unproven idea.

sections.heading: Set the test plan in advance
sections.content: She also cautions teams to define the hypothesis and how they will validate it before running an experiment, rather than fitting the data to a desired result afterward. If a team accepts greater risk of a false positive or false negative, she says it should think ahead about how to strengthen validation.
